events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Sam proposes Sam, Theo. As the leader, I will propose myself and Theo to establish a clean foundation for Mission 1.

I have concerns about this team. Sam proposed Sam and Theo, which means the leader put himself on the mission with no outside input. That is a self-selected team, and it gives the other players little reason to trust it. Mission 1 is our first real information point, so we should choose it carefully. I would like to hear from Leo and Isha on whether they think a team that includes the leader and one other player is the right foundation, or whether we should consider a different mix. I am not yet voting to reject, but I want this team justified before I approve it.

I think Sam's proposal is a reasonable starting point. As leader, including yourself on Mission 1 is standard practice, and Sam needs to put his own reputation behind this team if he believes in it. The question is whether Theo is the right second member. Theo, I would like to understand your perspective on why you feel confident about this team as it stands. Mission 1 with only two players carries significant weight, so both of you need to earn our trust here. I am open to this team but I want to hear from the rest of the table before I commit to approving it.

Arjun, on the very first proposal of the game, there is no prior discussion or voting record to pull from. A leader including themselves on Mission 1 is standard good play because I know my own alignment, guaranteeing at least one clean seat from my perspective. Framing that as an inherently suspicious move ignores how the game starts. Theo, seeing as Isha also wanted to hear from you, what do you make of Arjun's objection, and are you ready to approve and run this mission with me?

I understand Arjun's concern, but I do not think it justifies rejecting this team. On Mission 1 there is no voting record or mission result to work from, and a leader including himself is a standard way to put his own reputation behind the proposal. From my perspective, Sam and I are on the team, and I know I will play this mission cleanly. That does not prove Sam is good, but it means the team is not inherently unsafe just because the leader selected himself. Isha asked for my perspective, so to be direct: I am comfortable with this team as proposed. Arjun is right that we should justify the team, but I do not hear a concrete alternative concern beyond the usual first-mission skepticism. I am ready to approve and run this mission with Sam.

Before we vote, two points. Theo's response was clear and I accept it: a leader including himself on Mission 1 is normal, and Theo has committed to running the mission cleanly. Arjun's objection, though, was structural rather than substantive. He did not tell us anything specific about Theo that argues against him. He told us that the proposal was made with no outside input and that nobody else had tested it. That is still a fair concern, and I want it answered rather than talked past.

Here is what weighs on me. This is a two-player mission and one Fail card is all it takes to cost us the mission and hand Evil a point. So we are approving a very small team on no information, at the exact moment where a bad read is cheapest and most damaging. Theo's confidence tells us Theo will play well; it tells us nothing about whether Sam has read the table correctly on his first pick.

Sam, I want to ask you directly, since it is your proposal and your reputation: if you are confident enough to put your own name on the line, would you consider swapping Theo for Arjun, who at least has now shown he is thinking about the team and not just about his own position? And if you would rather keep Theo, can you tell us what specifically about Theo makes him the safer second seat than Arjun on this first mission?

I am accusing no one of bad faith and I am not rejecting on principle. I just want the leader to own the choice with an argument, not a first-mission formality.

Leo, to answer your question directly: I will not swap Theo for Arjun. Arjun's opening contribution was to attack standard first-mission protocol—casting suspicion on a leader proposing themselves when that is the most common and logical starting point in Avalon. That felt like manufacturing suspicion out of thin air rather than trying to build consensus. Theo, in contrast, responded reasonably, recognized that there is no prior data, and offered a clear and cooperative stance. I see no reason to discard a partner who has engaged constructively in favor of someone whose first reaction was to sow unnecessary doubt. I am confident in this proposal and will keep myself and Theo. Isha, seeing as Leo brought up this potential swap, what is your view on keeping this team versus Leo's idea of putting Arjun on?

Sam, to answer your question directly: I think keeping this team as proposed is reasonable. Mission 1 carries real risk with only two seats, but neither Theo nor you has given me a specific reason to doubt the team right now. Arjun raised a structural concern about how the team was formed, and I understand why Sam sees that as unnecessary suspicion, but I also think Leo has a fair point that Sam should be able to articulate why Theo specifically is the right second seat rather than leaning purely on first-mission protocol.

Theo, I appreciate your clear commitment to running this mission cleanly. That is exactly what we need to hear from someone on a two-player team with one Fail card deciding everything.

Here is where I land: I am inclined to approve Sam and Theo as proposed. Arjun's objection was fair discussion, not necessarily a red flag, and Leo's push for a stronger justification is reasonable. But Sam has now answered both concerns—explaining why he is keeping Theo and why he is not swapping in Arjun—and I find that sufficient for Mission 1. We have no prior data to go on, so at some point we have to trust the leader's initial read or this process will stall. I am ready to vote on this team as it stands.

Sam, I want to press you once more, and this time with a narrower question, because my earlier framing was about process and you answered it about process.

My question is specific: what do you actually know about Theo that you do not know about Arjun? Not what Theo said about Mission 1 having no voting history — that is true of everyone at this table. I mean something concrete. Has Theo done anything in this game, before this proposal, that gives you reason to believe he reads the table correctly? If you have that, say it. If you do not, then your choice of second seat rests entirely on the fact that Arjun criticized first-mission protocol and you found the criticism annoying.

Let me be clear about what I am and am not saying. I am not accusing Theo of being Evil. I have no evidence of that, and Isha's read that a leader including himself on Mission 1 is normal is fair, and I accept it. I am also not accusing you of bad faith; you are entitled to pick your own partner.

But the stakes are asymmetric and worth naming. One Fail card costs us this mission. Two seats, one of which is you, chosen before any data exists. If we are wrong, Evil gets its first point for free, and the next proposal comes from a leader who has now had two chances to explain himself and has chosen twice to explain himself in terms of protocol rather than people. The only player at this table who has actively interrogated the composition of the team is Arjun, and the leader's answer to that is that the questioning was inconvenient. That is not a reason to seat him, but it is a reason to explain the alternative.

So: either give me one concrete, Theo-specific reason — something about Theo you observed, or a judgment you made that you are willing to put your name behind beyond "it is standard" — and I will vote with you, or tell me plainly that you have nothing beyond protocol. If it is only protocol, then I am going to vote to reject this team, not because I think Theo is Evil, but because a two-seat mission on no information, defended with a formality rather than a reading, is the cheapest possible mistake for Evil to cash in. A rejection costs us a turn and gives the table a fresh proposal where the second seat can be chosen on the record by everyone, which is strictly better than approving a team the leader cannot justify on substance.

Sam, do you have a Theo-specific reason, or only the protocol argument? Please answer that question directly.

Leo, to be completely frank: demanding a concrete, Theo-specific game action prior to the very first proposal is setting an impossible standard that no player at this table could satisfy. On Mission 1, Turn 1, zero game actions have taken place. If that is your threshold for approving an opening team, then no initial proposal could ever be justified.

What we do have is how players have conducted themselves in this discussion. When Arjun spoke, his opening move was to manufacture suspicion against standard leader protocol. When Theo spoke, he was measured, cooperative, and clear in his commitment to run the mission cleanly. That demeanor is real, observable data from this table.

Rejecting this proposal does not generate better information; it simply resets the process and passes the pick to Arjun. Both Theo and Isha have stated they are satisfied and ready to vote. I am confident in this team, I am keeping myself and Theo, and I am ready to let the table decide on the vote.

Sam, you answered, so let me be precise about what I took from it, and then let me put the question where it actually belongs. You confirmed my suspicion. There is no Theo-specific reason. Your answer was: Theo behaved reasonably in this discussion, while Arjun's opening move was to "manufacture suspicion out of thin air." That is a description of temperament, not a read on alignment, and it is a choice you made because the questioning was inconvenient rather than because it was wrong. I want to be fair to you, Sam — you were candid, and I would rather have a candid protocol argument than a fake substance argument dressed up in confidence. So I am not accusing you of being Evil, and I am not accusing Theo of being Evil. I have no evidence of either. My objection is narrower and I am not moving off it: this is a two-seat mission, one Fail card decides it, and we are approving the second seat on no information at all. Here is what changed since my last turn, and it is the whole of what changed: nothing. No new game action, no new signal about Theo, no new signal about anyone. The only thing that was added to the record was Sam's reasoning, and the reasoning has now been shown to rest on protocol plus a dismissed objection. That is the answer to my question, and it is a "no." Isha, I want to ask you one specific question, because you are the vote that decides this and because you are the one who said Sam's answer was "sufficient." My question is not about whether first-mission protocol is normal — I accept that it is, and so do you. My question is this: what is the piece of information you now hold about Sam's read of this table that you did not hold when you first heard Leo's objection? If the answer is that the leader's protocol argument plus his opinion of Arjun's tone is enough, then say that plainly and vote for it — that is a legitimate position and I will accept it. But if the honest answer is that nothing has actually been added, then approving this team is approving a guess about Sam's judgment on the exact turn where a guess is cheapest to make and most expensive to pay for. A rejection does not destroy information; it hands the next pick to Arjun on the record, where a second seat can be chosen by a table that has at least seen one round of reasoning. Arjun, I know you have been characterized as the player who objected for the sake of objecting, and I want to say plainly that I think that characterization is unfair — your first concern was structural and legitimate and I want it answered, not talked past. Your read on how this team was assembled is the one that has not been tested. I am voting to reject this team,

Leo, I appreciate how thorough your questioning has been, but I want to respond directly to your challenge to me, because you asked what information I hold that I did not hold when I first heard your objection. The honest answer is: Sam has now been pressed twice by you on the same point and has given the same answer both times — that on Mission 1 with no prior data, the choice of Theo over Arjun rests on how each conducted themselves in this discussion. That is not a strong reason, but it is an honest one, and Sam did not dress it up as something it is not.

Here is what I think matters more than the protocol debate. You say rejection gives the table a better second seat chosen on the record. But look at what the record actually shows. Arjun's contribution was structural — he objected to the process of the pick, not to Theo as a person. If Arjun becomes leader next, what does he bring to the table that Sam does not? He will still have no additional information. The only thing a rejection gives us is a different leader with the same lack of data.

Meanwhile, you have spent this entire discussion pressing Sam on why Theo specifically, while never offering a concrete reason to prefer Arjun over Theo either. Your argument is not that Arjun is safer — you explicitly said you are not accusing Theo of anything. Your argument is that rejecting is structurally better than approving, and I do not see why that is true when the informational state will be identical after a rejection.

I am voting to approve Sam and Theo. I have heard everyone's concerns, including yours, Leo, and I do not think the case for rejection outweighs the cost of a stalled first mission.

Leo has pressed Sam on a real gap, and I do not think it has been closed. Sam's answers have been that Theo behaved well in discussion and that my objection was annoying. Good conduct in a debate is not evidence of alignment, and I said at the start that the team was chosen with no outside input. I am not voting to reject on principle, but I still want the leader to justify the second seat on substance. Theo, I accept that you intend to play cleanly. My question is narrower: if you were in Sam's position, with one Fail card deciding a two-player mission, what concrete reason would you give the table for choosing yourself over me?

Arjun, direct answer: if I were in Sam's position, I would not claim a concrete, Theo-specific or Arjun-specific alignment read from before any mission has happened, because no one can honestly have one yet. The only concrete thing a leader can say on the first proposal is: I know my own alignment, and I will play Success. That is why I would choose myself. For the second seat, the leader has to rely on how players have conducted themselves in discussion, not on prior game actions. Sam has now been pressed twice on that point, and his answer has stayed consistent: he preferred my cooperative response and my clear commitment to running the mission cleanly, and he did not like your opening objection. I understand why that is not a strong reason. It is not proof of alignment. But it is also not a fake claim of hidden knowledge. I am not accusing you of being Evil, Arjun. Your objection was legitimate and worth testing. I also do not think Leo's rejection case has produced a concrete alternative: a rejection changes the leader but does not create new mission data. Isha is right that the informational state would be nearly identical. As the second seat, I can only tell the table plainly: I will play this mission cleanly, and I am ready to approve Sam and Theo.

I am not voting to reject yet, but Sam's answers have been consistent in a way that does not yet address the question. Twice he has said Theo behaved cooperatively and that my objection was unhelpful. Conduct in discussion is a fair thing to weigh, but it does not show why Theo is the right second seat on a two-player mission. Theo, you have said you will play Success. That is a commitment from someone who is on the team, and the table cannot check it yet. Theo, which part of Sam's reasoning do you find most convincing, and would you still want this seat if the table had another option on the record?

Arjun, the most convincing part of Sam's reasoning is that he has stayed consistent under pressure: he is relying on how each player conducted themselves in this first discussion, and he has not pretended that gives him a concrete alignment read on me. I agree that is not strong evidence, and I have said plainly that I cannot prove my alignment before any mission card is played. On your second question, yes, I would still want this seat if Sam continues to choose me, because a two-seat Mission 1 requires the leader to make a decision, and I know I will play it cleanly. If Sam revised the team to another eligible player on the record, I would not treat that as an accusation against me; the leader owns the choice. My view remains that rejecting solely to change the leader does not create new mission data, while approving this team lets the table learn from an actual result.

Sam confirms Sam, Theo. After full discussion, Theo and Isha have demonstrated clear readiness to proceed, and no compelling alternative has been offered. I stand by this team and keep the proposal as Sam and Theo.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Theo proposes Theo, Sam, Isha. Mission 1 succeeded with Sam and me, and Isha consistently supported a justified first team without making an unsupported alignment claim. As a Loyal Servant, I know my own seat is clean, so I am keeping the successful Sam pairing and adding Isha for a three-player team.

Theo, this team has a shape problem, and it is worth naming before we vote, because the third seat is the only seat that is actually in play tonight.

Sam and Theo succeeded on Mission 1, and I am not going to relitigate that. But be honest about what that success proved. It was a two-seat mission where the leader seated himself. Whatever the result told us, it did not teach us anything about how a second or third seat should be filled — Sam's own presence made that mission close to a formality, and zero fail cards on a two-player team tells us very little about who was on it. So the third seat is where the real information is, and Theo, you have filled it with the one player at this table who has not yet made a single independent judgment.

Isha's contributions have been consistently deferred. She called Leo's objection fair, called Arjun's objection fair, called Sam's answer sufficient, and then approved. That is not a read on anyone — that is a position that agrees with whoever spoke most recently. On a three-player mission I want that seat occupied by a player who has shown he forms his own view of people and is willing to hold it against the room.

I want to be clear that I am not claiming Isha is Evil. I have no evidence of that, and I am not going to invent any. This is a criticism of demonstrated independence, not of alignment. What I do know is the record, and the record shows one player who has spent this game testing other people's reasoning and one player who has not yet tested anything.

Arjun, I want to hear this from you rather than from me: if you believe you are the better third seat for Mission 2 than Isha, tell the table what you think Mission 1 actually proved, and explain why a player who has spent the game interrogating team composition is a stronger choice on a three-player team than a player who has consistently deferred to it. If you cannot make that case, then Isha's deferential vote is at least a known quantity, and I will reconsider.

Theo, and to be direct about my own position: I am not ready to approve Isha as the third seat without that being answered.

Leo, you asked what Mission 1 proved, so here is my answer. A success with Sam and Theo tells us that neither of them played Fail, which is useful but limited. A two-player mission with a leader on it gives little information about how a third seat should be filled, and I agree with you on that. Where I disagree is on Isha. You say she only agrees with whoever spoke last, but that does not match the record. Early in this discussion she asked Theo directly why he felt confident in the team, and she was the first to ask Sam for a reason tied to the pick, not just to protocol. Agreeing with a reasonable answer is not the same as having no view. I also do not think a player's style of voting is a strong basis for rejecting a team on a three-player mission. If you want a stronger third seat, the test should be what each player has said about this specific team, not whether they pushed back in the same way you did. Isha, Leo says your approvals have been deferential and that you have not made an independent judgment. What is your reasoning for approving Sam and Theo after Leo's objection, and what would you bring to Mission 2 beyond agreeing with the table?

Arjun, direct answers to your two questions. First, my reasoning for approving Sam and Theo on Mission 1: I did not approve just because the table was leaning that way. I asked Theo directly why he felt confident in the team, which was my first contribution, and then I asked Sam directly to justify his pick after Leo's objection. When Sam gave a consistent answer grounded in discussion conduct rather than false claims of hidden knowledge, I found that honest enough for a first mission with zero prior data. That was my judgment, not deference. Second, what I bring beyond agreeing with the table: I have been the one asking players on or near the team to justify themselves directly, which is exactly what you both did to me just now. That is not passive agreement.

Leo, I want to respond to your criticism directly because you characterized my contributions as deferential. You said I called every objection fair and then approved. That is partially true, but you are framing a considered middle position as having no position at all. I called your objection fair and Arjun's objection fair because both were fair — they were not contradictory, and acknowledging that does not mean I was tracking whoever spoke last. I then explained precisely why I landed where I did: the informational state after rejection would be nearly identical, and the cost of stalling was real. That was an independent conclusion that contradicted your position. If deference means agreeing with someone after hearing their argument and finding it less persuasive than the alternative, then the word has lost its meaning.

On this specific team — Theo, Sam, Isha — I am comfortable being on the mission. Mission 1 succeeded with Sam, and Theo has been transparent about his reasoning throughout. I have no reason to doubt either of them at this stage, and I want us to keep building on the momentum from Mission 1.

Update first: Isha's answer satisfied me on the narrow point I raised about her voting style, and Arjun's correction about her first contribution was fair — she did ask Theo to justify himself before anyone else pressed him. I am not going to keep calling her deferential, because that is no longer an accurate description of the record, and the table deserves accuracy from me even when it costs me my argument.

So, Theo, what is left of my challenge is not about Isha's character. It is about how the third seat was chosen, and I will be honest that it is a structural argument, not an accusation of bad faith against anyone on this team.

Here is the record. Mission 1 succeeded on two seats with the leader on it. That result says very little about how to fill a third seat on a three-player mission, where one Fail card decides everything. Theo, you have filled that third seat with the pair that already succeeded, on the strength of momentum and your own stated wish to build on Sam. I understand that reasoning and I have no evidence against either of you. But we are approving the untested seat, and two of the three seats are players whose judgment we have never seen applied to a different pairing.

And here is what I think is actually on the table, stated plainly: the next leader after Theo is Arjun. If this team is rejected, the second and third seats get filled on the record by the one player at this table who has spent the game testing other people's reasoning against specific claims and saying plainly when the answer is missing. Every other player here has asked for justification; Arjun has judged justification. That is a different skill, and on a three-player mission where a single card decides it, we have no read on it at all. A rejection costs us one turn of progress and gains us a proposal that has actually been argued, which is a trade I am prepared to make.

Arjun, one thing you owe the table, and you have still not given it: not another defense of Isha, but your own case for why you are the right third seat for Mission 2 — and specifically what you think Mission 1 actually proved and what it did not prove. Make that case now, on the record, and I will vote to reject this team so the third seat is filled by someone whose judgment on this exact question has been stated openly. If your case is weak, say so plainly and I will reconsider — I am not buying a seat on an unstated read, from either side.

Leo asked what Mission 1 proved, so here is my answer. It proved that Sam and Theo did not play Fail, and nothing more. A success on a two-player mission with the leader on it tells us little about how a third seat should be filled, and I agree with Leo on that. It also does not show what either of them would have done with a Fail card under real pressure. Theo, your proposal keeps Sam and adds Isha. That is momentum from Mission 1, not a new test of the third seat. On a three-player mission where one Fail card decides everything, I would expect the proposal to explain why this seat is the strongest available choice. So far the case has been mostly about Isha's conduct in discussion, not about anything she has shown on this team. I have asked substantive questions from the start and have been willing to say when a justification is missing. I am not asking for a seat on reputation. I am asking that the third seat be chosen on the record by the table, rather than carried over from a mission that taught us little about it. If Theo can give a concrete reason for Isha over the other eligible players, I will weigh it fairly. If not, I will not approve this team.

Arjun, you asked for a concrete reason for Isha over the other eligible players. Here it is: Isha directly asked me to justify my confidence before anyone else pressed me, then directly pressed Sam after Leo's objection, and when Leo challenged her, she gave an independent conclusion about the informational cost of rejection rather than simply echoing the last speaker. That is a specific, observable contribution to this exact team question. Leo's correction that she is not merely deferential is fair. I also did not choose Isha because she approved me; I chose her because she tested the first team and then reasoned through the rejection tradeoff.

On Mission 1: I agree it proved only that Sam and I submitted success, not that either of us is proven good. I know my own seat is clean. Keeping Sam preserves a successful pairing; adding Isha adds a player who has questioned both members of that pairing directly. A rejection would change the leader, but it would not create new mission cards or new alignment data. Arjun's testing is valuable, but testing alone is not proof of alignment, and I have no concrete evidence against him or Leo.

I am not accusing anyone of bad faith. My case is narrower: this team has a successful pair plus the player who has most directly tested that pair. Unless someone presents a concrete reason that Isha is unsafe beyond style or that Sam's success is meaningless, I stand by Theo, Sam, Isha.

Update first, because the record has changed since my last turn and I owe the table accuracy. Arjun answered the question I put to him, and he answered it on the record, which is what I asked for. Mission 1 proved exactly one thing: Sam and Theo did not play Fail. It proved nothing about how a third seat should be filled, and Arjun and I agree on that point. What Arjun added beyond Isha's answer is a judgment rather than a request for judgment: he has been the player willing to say plainly that a justification was missing, and he said it about this exact proposal, to this exact leader, in this exact discussion. Isha's answer was a defense of her own reasoning style. Arjun's answer was a case for a seat. Theo, I want to be honest about what I am asking for, because you deserve a straight request rather than a debate about style. You asked me for a concrete reason for Isha over the other eligible players, and you gave three: she asked me to justify myself first, she pressed Sam, and she reached an independent conclusion about the cost of rejection. I accept all three as true. What I notice is that every one of them describes behavior in this discussion, not alignment, and that the reason I never got to make was that I was asked to state a Theo-specific or Arjun-specific game action that does not exist yet. The same standard applied to you would have blocked Isha too, and you were not blocked, and Isha knows why. So the table has a team of Theo, Sam, Isha in which two seats are a proven-good pair and the third seat is a player whose every vote has tracked the most recent strong argument rather than her own read of the people on it. Arjun is not a claim I am inventing; he has made his case for the third seat explicitly, on substance, in public, and it is stronger than the case for Isha. He has demonstrated exactly the property that matters on a three-player mission where a single Fail card decides everything: he reads a team and says what he sees instead of mirroring the room. Theo, my direct question to you as leader: now that Arjun has put a concrete case on the record for the third seat and has withdrawn from the pure process objection to a substantive one, do you have any alignment-based reason to prefer Isha over Arjun for Mission 2? If you do not, please revise the team to Theo, Sam, Arjun. If you do, state it, and I will weigh it fairly. I am still not accusing anyone of bad faith, and Isha, I want to say clearly that I do not think you are Evil and I have no evidence of that. I will keep Theo, Sam, Isha. Leo asked whether I have an alignment-based reason to prefer Isha over Arjun, and I will answer plainly: I do not have private alignment evidence against Arjun, and I am not accusing him of being Evil. But the same is true of Isha. Mission 1 proved only that Sam and I did not play Fail; it did not prove either of us is good, and it did not create new alignment data about any third seat. So the choice must rest on the public record of this discussion. On that record, Isha directly asked me to justify my confidence before anyone else pressed me, directly pressed Sam after Leo's objection, and then gave her own conclusion about the cost of rejecting rather than simply echoing the room. Arjun has also contributed substantively, and I respect his questioning, but his case for the third seat is largely a case about testing style, not alignment. Testing alone is not proof of goodness, just as cooperation alone is not proof of goodness. A rejection would change the leader but would not create mission cards or alignment information before the next vote. I have no concrete evidence that Isha is unsafe, and I have no concrete evidence that Arjun is safer. Given that, I stand by the successful Sam pairing and the player who has most directly tested that pairing in public. I am not accusing Leo or Arjun of bad faith. I am saying that I will not revise the team based on a standard that no player could meet on Mission 1.

I fully support Theo's proposal of Theo, Sam, and Isha. Looking at how this discussion has unfolded, there is a very obvious pattern worth noting: Leo was the sole player to vote against Mission 1, and now on Mission 2, Leo has spent almost his entire time maneuvering to get Arjun into the third seat at the expense of Isha. Arjun, in turn, has happily stepped up to claim that seat. We already know that Mission 1 succeeded cleanly with Theo and myself. Isha has demonstrated solid, independent logic from the start—she questioned both of us before deciding to approve, and she correctly recognized the flaw in Leo's desire to reject without new information. Replacing Isha with Arjun, based purely on Leo's persistent advocacy, makes no sense for the Good team. Theo has made the right call in holding firm, and I am completely ready to approve Theo, Sam, and Isha.

Sam has just named the pattern I was about to name myself, so let me add to it rather than repeat it. Leo, you were the sole vote to reject Mission 1. That team succeeded with zero fail cards. Now on Mission 2, you have spent the entire discussion trying to remove me from the third seat and replace me with Arjun, while never once arguing that Arjun is safer based on any concrete evidence. You have explicitly stated you have no evidence I am Evil. So your entire case is not about my alignment — it is about preference for one player's debating style over another's on a team where no alignment data exists either way.

Let me address Arjun's argument directly, because he and Leo are making complementary moves. Arjun says he has shown better judgment than me by identifying missing justifications. I have identified missing justifications too — I pressed Theo before anyone else did, I pressed Sam after Leo objected, and I reached my own independent conclusion about the cost of rejection. The difference between us is not that one of us questions and the other does not. The difference is that Arjun has used his questioning to argue himself onto this team, which is a different activity entirely.

Theo's reasoning for keeping me is sound: I tested the first pairing directly and reasoned through the rejection tradeoff independently. That is exactly what you want from a third seat on a three-player mission. Leo and Arjun have built a campaign around style preference, not safety concerns. I am ready to approve Theo, Sam, and Isha.

Sam, you have now treated Leo's objection as a pattern and tied it to Isha's defense, but you have not answered the substance. Leo and I have both asked the same thing from the start: what concrete reason puts a specific player in the third seat? Theo's answer is that Isha questioned him, pressed you, and reasoned about rejection. Those are conduct points, and Isha has repeated them. I accept that questioning is not proof of alignment, and I have never said it was. My position has not changed. I will not approve a three-player mission because a seat was carried over from a two-player success. Mission 1 proved only that Sam and Theo did not play Fail. Sam, you say Isha independently tested the pair, but she also told us she found your answer sufficient and approved. Which of her points shows she tests teammates rather than follows the most recent strong speaker? I am not accusing Isha of being Evil, and I have no evidence that she is. My objection is that this seat was chosen on momentum, and the table has not heard a reason beyond conduct. If you can name a concrete basis for Isha over the other eligible players, I will weigh it fairly. Until then, I am not approving this team.

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
